query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small, controlled amount of aluminum to a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy, followed by an aging heat treatment to induce nanoscale precipitates, will improve the alloy’s elevated-temperature mechanical properties compared to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy containing at least five elements (each between 5–35 at%) with Ti and Ni as the dominant constituents, produced without any targeted precipitate-forming additions or specialized heat treatments.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 3–5 at% aluminum into the alloy composition and apply an aging heat treatment (e.g., heating at 850°C for 1–2 hours) to stimulate the formation of nanoscale, coherent precipitates.
generation.conditions: The aging treatment is conducted in an inert atmosphere with the subsequent mechanical tests performed at elevated temperatures (around 900°C) where precipitate stability is expected.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of nanoscale, coherent precipitates (potentially Ni3Al or TiAl-based phases) uniformly distributed in the matrix.
generation.mechanism: The nanoscale precipitates impede dislocation motion at high temperatures, thereby increasing yield strength and improving creep resistance via a precipitation strengthening mechanism.
generation.predicted_outcome: The intervention is predicted to result in roughly a 10–20% improvement in yield strength and enhanced creep resistance at high temperature relative to the baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: The same titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy without aluminum addition and without the aging treatment.
generation.boundary: The intervention is applicable within the compositional regime (all elements maintained between 5–35 at%), for alloys where Ti and Ni are primary constituents, and for service temperatures where the precipitates remain stable (likely up to around 900°C).
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of strengthening depends on the coherence and distribution of the precipitates, which may vary with slight changes in processing parameters. It is also uncertain whether the proposed aluminum addition will produce the desired precipitate without detrimental phase formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples: one set of the titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy with 3–5 at% aluminum added and subjected to the aging heat treatment (e.g., 850°C for 1–2 hours) to encourage precipitate formation, and a control set without aluminum addition or aging. Characterize the microstructure (using TEM or similar) to verify precipitate formation and then conduct mechanical tests (such as tensile and creep tests) at an elevated temperature (around 900°C).
measurements: Microstructural analysis confirming precipitate presence and characteristics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-modified and aged alloy does not exhibit at least a 10% statistically significant improvement in yield strength or reduction in creep rate compared to the baseline alloy, or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal the intended nanoscale precipitates, then the hypothesis will be falsified.
